title: fix(watch): prevent overlapping runs and other run lifecycle bugs

### Description

The background here is that we used to be plagued by very seldom failures of certain watch mode tests. Running my agent to do a stress test first uncovered a race condition, and that led to a rabbit hole of fixes.

This fixes a rare watch mode flake where the second of two overlapping runs emitted its `START` event while the active run was still between `BUNDLE_START` and `BUNDLE_END`, together with several related gaps in the run lifecycle that turned up while reproducing it. Each fix comes with a regression test that failed without it:

- **Overlapping runs:** invalidations that arrived while change events were still being announced — e.g. while an async `watchChange` hook was running — started a second run cycle that overlapped with the current one, interleaving watcher events and removing the per-run plugin event listeners mid-run.
- **Lost plugin listeners:** a rerun that had nothing left to rebuild still emitted a `restart` event and started an empty run, removing the plugin event listeners of the last completed run without a replacement.
- **Lost announcements:** changes that arrived during a failed run were wiped from the pending change events by the error reporting, so their `watchChange` hooks never ran even though the next run still rebuilt from them.
- **No recovery after a failed run:** a rerun requested during a run that then failed was never honored — the watcher idled with an invalidated task until another change happened to arrive.
- **Builds after close:** closing the watcher did not stop a cycle that was already announcing changes, so a build was started and discarded after the close. The same applied to closes that arrived before a run's first build or between the builds of a multi-config run.
- **Dropped early close:** closing the watcher immediately after `rollup.watch()` was silently lost because the watcher is set up asynchronously — it was still constructed, built once, and then kept running forever. The close is now remembered, the watcher is never constructed, and the `close` event is emitted right away.
- **Interleaved event listeners:** a change that arrived while an async `ERROR` or `END` listener of the previous run was still executing was announced and rebuilt right away, although rollup waits for returned listener promises everywhere else. The next cycle now starts only once the pending listeners resolved.
- **Failed listener siblings:** an event listener that failed made the event emission reject right away — a synchronously throwing one even skipped the remaining listeners — so the next cycle could start and announce changes while other listeners were still pending. Emissions now invoke every listener and wait for all of them before rethrowing the first failure.
- **Lost watch hooks:** the `watchChange` and `closeWatcher` hooks of every graph were per-run emitter listeners that were all removed right before the next run. When that run failed before building a new graph — e.g. when an event listener or the `options` hook threw — or when a multi-config run only rebuilt some configs, the affected plugins missed all later changes and their `closeWatcher` hook was skipped on close. Each task now keeps the hooks of its latest graph, handed over when that graph is created, and the watcher calls them next to the `change` and `close` events. Plugin hooks are no longer event listeners, so `removeAllListeners()` no longer silences them on a live watcher, and changes are no longer announced to plugins once the watcher is closed.
- **Uncleaned close:** a failing `close` listener or `closeWatcher` hook made `close()` reject before the listener cleanup; since a closed watcher ignored further close calls, its listeners were retained forever. The cleanup now runs even when closing fails, and closed tasks drop the hooks of their latest graph — including a graph finished after the close — so a retained watcher no longer keeps a build graph alive.

All scenarios are covered by 24 regression tests in `test/watch/index.js`, each one red without its fix. To make the lifecycle consistent, one wrapper now owns the running flag, the error reporting and the rerun handling for every run cycle.
